Learn.introBody: Hebrew has 22 letters. Each letter has its own sound.
Learn.hoverHint: Hover a letter to hear ah. The patach mark stays hidden for now.
Learn.cursiveHint: Hebrew also has a cursive hand for notes. We will come back to that later.
Learn.leaveBody: Progress in this level will be lost.
Learn.nikudBody: <bold>Letters</bold> represent the consonant, and the vowels are the <blue>nikud</blue>.

Learn.patachBody: Patach makes the ah sound. Hover a letter to hear it.

Learn.levelTwoDoneBody: Those first five letters are in place. Level 3 is next.
Learn.levelTwoIntro: Now the letters start making words.
Learn.fishBody: דָג means fish. Change the nikud and the sound changes: dag, dehg, deeg, dohg.
Learn.sofitIntro: There are five letters that have a final shape. They are the same, this is just how we write them when the letter appears at the end of a word.
Learn.sofitWhen: Use the final shape when that letter is the last letter of a word.
Learn.vowelBody: Hebrew vowels are the nikud marks. They are not extra letters the way a, e, i, o, and u are in English.
Learn.silentBody: א and ע often just carry the vowel. He at the end of a word is often silent. ו and י can hold the sounds oh, oo, and ee.
Learn.wordsDone: Those words are in your Known words deck.
Learn.flashcardsUnlockedBody: You finished level 4. Flashcards are open. Study there to keep these words.

Learn.nikudInfoIntro: Each mark on ב changes the sound. Click a mark to hear it.

letterNotes.aleph: Usually silent today. It carries the vowel written with it.
letterNotes.bet: B with a dot inside, v without it.
letterNotes.gimel: Makes a g sound, like in go.
letterNotes.he: Makes an h sound. At the end of a word it is often silent.
letterNotes.vav: Makes a v sound. It also carries the vowels o and u.
letterNotes.zayin: Makes a z sound, like in zebra.
letterNotes.chet: A throaty ch sound, like the end of Bach.
letterNotes.tet: A t sound. Today it sounds the same as tav.
letterNotes.yod: A y sound. The smallest letter, and it often carries an i vowel.
letterNotes.kaf: K with a dot inside, a soft kh without it. It changes shape to ך at the end of a word.
letterNotes.lamed: An l sound. The tallest letter, rising above the line.
letterNotes.mem: An m sound. It changes shape to ם at the end of a word.
letterNotes.nun: An n sound. It changes shape to ן at the end of a word.
letterNotes.samekh: An s sound, written as a closed loop.
letterNotes.ayin: Usually silent today. It carries the vowel written with it.
letterNotes.pe: P with a dot inside, f without it. It changes shape to ף at the end of a word.
letterNotes.tsadi: A ts sound, like in cats. It changes shape to ץ at the end of a word.
letterNotes.kuf: A k sound. Its leg drops below the line.
letterNotes.reish: An r sound, said in the throat.
letterNotes.shin: Sh with a dot on the right, s with a dot on the left.
letterNotes.tav: A t sound. The last letter of the aleph-bet.
letterNotes.kafSofit: Final kaf. It comes at the end of a word and sounds like kh.
letterNotes.memSofit: Final mem. It comes at the end of a word.
letterNotes.nunSofit: Final nun. It comes at the end of a word.
letterNotes.peSofit: Final pe. It comes at the end of a word and sounds like f.
letterNotes.tsadiSofit: Final tsadi. It comes at the end of a word.

Learn.readingIntroBody: Now we are going to start reading real Hebrew words and forming sentences. Your vocabulary will really start to grow with useful words, which is essential to becoming fluent and confident.
Learn.readingIntroNikud: In modern Hebrew, nikud is only written some of the time. We use it here only where it helps, and words will start to look familiar and recognisable without it.
Learn.readingIntroDecks: Every word you learn is added to your Known words deck. Practise them any time in the Decks tab.
Learn.shelUse: It comes after the thing that is owned. <he>הַכֶּלֶב שֶׁלִּי</he> is literally “the dog of me”, which means my dog. The owned thing usually takes <he>הַ</he> (the) in front.
Learn.shelEndings: An ending on של shows who the owner is:
Learn.shelStage1Body: These three endings show whose thing it is: mine, his, or hers. Hear each one, then build six sentences.
Learn.shelStage2Body: <he>שלנו</he> means ours. <he>זה</he> is for one thing; <he>אלה</he> is for more than one. Hebrew plurals often end in <he>ים</he> or <he>ות</he>.
Learn.pluralSuffixes: Masculine plurals often take ים. Feminine plurals often take ות. Example: אלה הכלבים שלנו — these are our dogs.
Learn.shelStage3Body: שלכם is yours when speaking to a group of men, or a mixed group. שלכן is yours when speaking to a group of women.
Learn.shelStage4Body: שלהם is theirs for a group of men, or a mixed group. שלהן is theirs for a group of women.
Learn.sentenceBuildPrompt: Listen, then drag the words into the right order to form the sentence.
Learn.examBuildPrompt: Listen, then put the words in order. Some words do not belong in the sentence.
Learn.eatBody: This is a present-tense verb that takes את. Hear the masculine, feminine, and plural forms.
Learn.etHaBody: Compare <he>הוא אוכל שוקולד</he> with <he>הוא אוכל את השוקולד</he>. When the object has the, Hebrew uses את before it. That את ה pattern is important.
Learn.drinkLearnBody: The same present-tense pattern: masculine, feminine, and plurals. Verbs with ל, על, and מ come later.
Learn.readBody: Another present-tense verb that takes את. Hear the masculine, feminine, and plural forms.
Learn.readNounsBody: These nouns go with לקרוא. Hear each one, then build sentences that use them.
Learn.writeBody: לכתוב also takes את. Hear the four present-tense forms. The sentences use מכתב and סיפור from the last level.
Learn.loveBody: לאהוב means to like or to love. The present tense follows the same masculine, feminine, and plural pattern.
Learn.loveNounsBody: A song takes את when it is definite. Music, like water, does not need את.

AlephBet.title: Aleph Bet
AlephBet.scriptInfo: The front of each card is standard script, the square print letters used in books and on signs. The back is cursive, the handwritten form used for notes.
AlephBet.studySetup: Choose how many cards. Flip each one, then mark whether you know it.
AlephBet.practiceLettersHint: See a letter and recall its name.
AlephBet.practiceNikudHint: See a letter with a vowel mark and read the sound.
AlephBet.scriptPrintHint: Square letters used in books and on signs.
AlephBet.scriptBothHint: A mix of standard and cursive cards.
AlephBet.drawHint: Trace the letter. Lift the pen between parts, and stay on the shape.
AlephBet.cursiveSettingHint: Practice the handwritten letters instead of the standard print.
AlephBet.arrowHint: Left arrow for Don't know, right arrow for Know.
AlephBet.loanNote: This is not one of the 22 letters. Hebrew uses it to spell sounds borrowed from other languages.
AlephBet.sofitTip: Final letters are used a little like capital letters in English, but they come at the end of a word instead of at the start of a sentence.

aleph.description: Aleph has no consonant sound. You pronounce the vowel written with it.
aleph.note: It can carry any vowel, so these words do not all start with the same sound.

bet.description: Bet says b with a dot inside, and v without one.

gimel.description: Gimel says g, as in go.

he.description: He says h. At the end of a word it is often silent.

vav.description: Vav says v. It also writes the vowels o and u.

chet.description: Chet says kh, a rough sound in the back of the throat, like the ch in the Scottish loch.
chet.note: In modern Israeli Hebrew this is the same sound as kaf without a dot.

tet.description: Tet says t. In modern Hebrew it sounds the same as tav.

yod.description: Yod says y, as in yes. It also writes the vowel i.

kaf.description: Kaf says k with a dot inside, and kh without one.

kafSofit.description: This is kaf at the end of a word. Final kaf usually says kh.
kafSofit.note: Its value is 20, the same as kaf. In gematria this final form can also count as 500.

memSofit.description: This is mem at the end of a word. It says m.
memSofit.note: Its value is 40, the same as mem. In gematria this final form can also count as 600.

nunSofit.description: This is nun at the end of a word. It says n.
nunSofit.note: Its value is 50, the same as nun. In gematria this final form can also count as 700.

samekh.description: Samekh says s, the same sound as sin, the s-form of shin.

ayin.description: Ayin is silent in modern Hebrew. You pronounce only the vowel written with it.
ayin.note: Older Hebrew had a deep sound in the throat here.

pe.description: Pe says p with a dot inside, and f without one.

peSofit.description: This is pe at the end of a word. Final pe usually says f.
peSofit.note: Its value is 80, the same as pe. In gematria this final form can also count as 800.

tsadi.description: Tsadi says ts, as at the end of bits.

tsadiSofit.description: This is tsadi at the end of a word. It says ts.
tsadiSofit.note: Its value is 90, the same as tsadi. In gematria this final form can also count as 900.

kuf.description: Kuf says k, the same sound as kaf with a dot.

reish.description: Reish says r. In Israeli Hebrew it is made at the back of the mouth.

shin.description: Shin says sh when the dot is on the upper right. With the dot on the upper left it is sin, and it says s.

gimelGeresh.description: Gimel with a geresh, the small mark beside it, says j as in jeans.

zayinGeresh.description: Zayin with a geresh says zh, the sound in measure, or the French j.

tsadiGeresh.description: Tsadi with a geresh says ch as in chips.
